Time-Domain Terahertz Spectroscopy Tools

This small library is designed mainly for processing time-domain data in transmission optics. It includes:

  • signal (kernel) deconvolution;
  • seamless conversion between the time and frequency domains;
  • projections from linear to circular bases;
  • extraction of material parameters (absorption, refractive index, etc.), including multiple-beam propagation and Fresnel losses;
  • advanced 1D phase unwrapping guided by the Kramers–Kronig relation;
  • optical-response modeling for thin and thick slabs;
  • band-pass filtering and apodization of time traces;

All functions are strongly typed but also support multiple input patterns: time-domain data is automatically converted to the frequency domain if needed. Iterative solvers are implemented in OpenCL, with C functions running on the CPU as a fallback and a WL implementation serving as a secondary fallback if the C version fails to load.

Github repository https://github.com/JerryI/THzTDSTools

Let's get started!

Material parameter extraction

Here is an example of a typical THz-TDS workflow using data measured with a Toptica TeraFlash (2013) spectrometer.

The sample and reference (empty-aperture) signals must be assigned exact units ("Seconds" or "Millimeters" of delay-stage motion).

{sam, ref} = QuantityArray[#, {"Picoseconds", 1}] &/@ {sam, ref};

Now we can plot both channels and adjust the range to the region with the highest SNR.

In linear-response theory, the resulting sample signal is the convolution of the IRF(or transmission function) and the probe signal (reference):

sample(τ)=reference(τ) ∗ t(τ)\text{sample}(\tau) = \text{reference}(\tau)~\ast~t(\tau)sample(τ)=reference(τ) ∗ t(τ)

The function t(τ)t(\tau)t(τ), or its Fourier transform t(ω)t(\omega)t(ω), contains all information about the sample.

NOTE

We recommend performing all transformations in the time domain whenever possible.

Let's explore this:

t = DeconvolveTraces[sam, ref]; ListLinePlot[t // ToStandardOpticsUnits, Frame->True, PlotRange->Full, PlotRange->Full, FrameLabel->{"\[Tau] (ps)", "t(\[Tau])"}, PlotLabel->"Time-domain"] TD2FD[t] //FrequencySpectrumTrim // ToStandardOpticsUnits; ListLinePlot[%[[All, {1,2}]], Frame->True, PlotRange->Full, PlotRange->Full, FrameLabel->{"\[Omega] (THz)", "|t(\[Omega])|"}, PlotLabel->"Frequency-domain"] (*VB[*)(FrontEndRef["Fc7eed9b0-7f89-40c4-bc1c-7b932ee6a9cf"])(*,*)(*"1:eJxTTMoPSmNkYGAoZgESHvk5KRCeEJBwK8rPK3HNS3GtSE0uLUlMykkNVgUJJ5unpqZYJhnomqdZWOqaGCSb6CYlGybrmidZGhulppolWianAQCpMha5"*)(*]VB*) (*VB[*)(FrontEndRef["F552b0c1e-fe00-454e-b2f2-33314c226776"])(*,*)(*"1:eJxTTMoPSmNkYGAoZgESHvk5KRCeEJBwK8rPK3HNS3GtSE0uLUlMykkNVgUJm5oaJRkkG6bqpqUaGOiamJqk6iYZpRnpGhsbG5okGxmZmZubAQCWGxVJ"*)(*]VB*)

The modulus of t(ω)t(\omega)t(ω) corresponds to the transmission spectrum. Given the thickness of the measured sample and the aperture difference between the sample and reference measurements, the absorption coefficient α(ω)\alpha(\omega)α(ω) can be estimated:

EstimateMaterialParameter["\[Alpha]"][t, Quantity[0.6, "Millimeters"], "Gain"->1.2, Method->"Basic"]; Select[% // ToStandardOpticsUnits, (#[[1]]>0.3 && #[[1]]<3.65) &]; ListLinePlot[%, Frame->True, PlotRange->Full, FrameLabel->{"\[Omega] (THz)", "\[Alpha] (1/cm)"}] (*VB[*)(FrontEndRef["F5f27967e-0cb4-4b4f-8ffe-653bb05fbf41"])(*,*)(*"1:eJxTTMoPSmNkYGAoZgESHvk5KRCeEJBwK8rPK3HNS3GtSE0uLUlMykkNVgUJm6YZmVuamafqGiQnmeiaJJmk6VqkpaXqmpkaJyUZmKYlpZkYAgCeShZV"*)(*]VB*)

Advanced methods

The "Basic" method assumes:

α(ω)=−16n02(n0+1)42d log ∣t(ω)∣,\alpha(\omega) = - \frac{16 n_0^2}{(n_0+1)^4} \frac{2}{d} ~log~|t(\omega)|,α(ω)=−(n0​+1)416n02​​d2​ log ∣t(ω)∣,

where n0n_0n0​ is the average refractive index, estimated automatically from the pulse delay. This equation holds for optically thick samples with strong absorption. In the general case, however, α\alphaα is:

α(ω)=2ω ℑ n(ω)c\alpha(\omega) = \frac{2 \omega~\Im~n(\omega)}{c}α(ω)=c2ω ℑ n(ω)​

To estimate nnn from the complex transmission function ttt, one must iteratively solve the Fresnel equations: [Withayachumnankul, W., Ferguson, B., Rainsford, T., Mickan, S. P., & Abbott, D. (2005). Material parameter extraction for terahertz time-domain spectroscopy using fixed-point iteration. Proceedings of SPIE, 5649, 142–153. doi.org]

The most general material response for a slab-like sample is modeled as:

t(ω)=4n(ω)[1+n(ω)]2⏟interface transmissionexp⁡ ⁣[iωLc(n(ω)−1)]⏟single pass11−(n(ω)−1n(ω)+1)2exp⁡ ⁣(2iωLcn(ω))⏟Fabry–Peˊrot termt(\omega)= \underbrace{\frac{4 n(\omega)}{[1+ n(\omega)]^2}}_{\text{interface transmission}} \underbrace{\exp\!\left[i\frac{\omega L}{c}\bigl( n(\omega)-1\bigr)\right]}_{\text{single pass}} \underbrace{\frac{1}{ 1-\left(\frac{ n(\omega)-1}{ n(\omega)+1}\right)^2 \exp\!\left(2i\frac{\omega L}{c} n(\omega)\right) }}_{\text{Fabry–Pérot term}}t(ω)=interface transmission[1+n(ω)]24n(ω)​​​single passexp[icωL​(n(ω)−1)]​​Fabry–Peˊrot term1−(n(ω)+1n(ω)−1​)2exp(2icωL​n(ω))1​​​

Phase unwrapping

TD2FD stores the principal Fourier phase in the range from −π-\pi−π to π\piπ. A sampled wrapped phase does not, by itself, tell us how many full 2π2\pi2π turns occur between frequency bins. The usual nearest-neighbor unwrap therefore becomes unreliable when the phase changes rapidly or the transmission reaches a deep minimum (for example, near a sharp excitation). This library offers a Kramers–Kronig (KK)-guided method that uses the measured magnitude to help choose those turns.

Here are all the built-in methods for comparison:

$methods = {None, "Basic", "KK", "KKGuided", "KKGuidedMultiscale"}; UnwrapPhase[t, Method->#, "RemoveLinearPhase"->True] &/@ $methods; ToStandardOpticsUnits /@ FrequencySpectrumTrim /@ %; ListLinePlot[%[[All, All, {1,3}]], Frame->True, PlotRange->{{0.25, 3.0}, {-5,20}}, FrameLabel->{"\[Omega] (THz)", "\[Phi]"}, PlotLegends->(ToString/@$methods), PlotLabel->"Phase unwrapping"] (*VB[*)(Legended[ToExpression[FrontEndRef["F81198e4a-2bba-4332-adbc-d0d1b92feaf8"], InputForm], Placed[LineLegend[{Directive[PointSize[0.006944444444444445], RGBColor[0.24, 0.6, 0.8], AbsoluteThickness[2]], Directive[PointSize[0.006944444444444445], RGBColor[0.95, 0.627, 0.1425], AbsoluteThickness[2]], Directive[PointSize[0.006944444444444445], RGBColor[0.455, 0.7, 0.21], AbsoluteThickness[2]], Directive[PointSize[0.006944444444444445], RGBColor[0.922526, 0.385626, 0.209179], AbsoluteThickness[2]], Directive[PointSize[0.006944444444444445], RGBColor[0.578, 0.51, 0.85], AbsoluteThickness[2]]}, {"None", "Basic", "KK", "KKGuided", "KKGuidedMultiscale"}, LegendMarkers -> {{False, Automatic}, {False, Automatic}, {False, Automatic}, {False, Automatic}, {False, Automatic}}, Joined -> {True, True, True, True, True}, LabelStyle -> {}, LegendLayout -> "Column"], After, Identity]])(*,*)(*"1:eJzNVM1rVDEQ31ZbtSjY4qGHWlEQvCy6uz1sDzVs7bro7mrdVM/mvUw0NE1skqduEW/9I/Qi6E2kN6FnDxY8iIigoIL1C6QoeBG8Nclza30ICsJiDkMy+WVmfvOR/ZFqsS25XM7scuIchytTECtNrNJ4m9M04AJIWkwhA05UKXd3Hsh6vG7IieNaSVuVtHoV4sSSSAA+6NXlQmG8DGMkX4wikh8rlYp5QqM4T4/QQjReZEBYmfV6K1udaCXu3Xa/AUJPS9EO2hmdQAbjw8AgIA6uTJ93RYSBNMh+J6YFiYGy/k7QDS4hZcL6OqYa3Nj0xQ4nprh29vhlSFl51bTi0mK+AHrvyvzIyvw1lMJDiLXJY0oorZdHF9fOLD9GuhTWO6Rv3vDrE0oNDTpRiYwSiYWZizyelWAM93z+3TcL6wvSd78+bUa73yM9MfD8zqWJB13wvc/THn2NfgTxEenVhT1LtdVHXfD97P63o2cXPyP96vCte8NLL5A+VOu5ff5hN3x/eHLg5ffrb5Fuhcq/6RR+7c++f+k87DenlATs1ZPE8Bh7VL0eRqBeryWcAsVDmw7NRFhuYiIyAxFGN23vJtGzoE2my3s3n37OS2BdSayaI5bH/z8qcPUzfdJVCjKjvPFZ/M0mYzN8ESQCgW3bJTf3++QF6M6NVDdIWyUW+3hcayRzMhCoMOvy70t4goK03LbXAZqScUY="*)(*]VB*)

The difference between KKGuided and KKGuidedMultiscale is that the latter also considers neighboring bins to verify that the local background level remains consistent. The latter method outperforms the others in this particular case.

Iterative method

By setting Method to "Iterative", we can estimate the material parameters more accurately by using almost all of the information available in the measured time traces. Let's compare the two methods.

unwrapped = UnwrapPhase[t, Method->"KKGuidedMultiscale"]; ListLinePlot[{ EstimateMaterialParameter["\[Alpha]", unwrapped, Quantity[0.6, "Millimeters"], "Gain"->1.2], EstimateMaterialParameter["\[Alpha]", unwrapped, Quantity[0.6, "Millimeters"], Method->"Iterative", "Gain"->1.2] }, PlotRange->{{0.2,4.0}, {-20,160}}, Frame->True, FrameLabel->{"f (THz)", "\[Alpha] (1/cm)"}, PlotLegends->{"-LogT / d", "Iterative solver for n and k"}] (*VB[*)(Legended[ToExpression[FrontEndRef["Fae25aaa2-2470-4814-8daf-9ef6d77c933a"], InputForm], Placed[LineLegend[{Directive[PointSize[0.006944444444444445], RGBColor[0.24, 0.6, 0.8], AbsoluteThickness[2]], Directive[PointSize[0.006944444444444445], RGBColor[0.95, 0.627, 0.1425], AbsoluteThickness[2]]}, {"-LogT / d", "Iterative solver for n and k"}, LegendMarkers -> {{False, Automatic}, {False, Automatic}}, Joined -> {True, True}, LabelStyle -> {}, LegendLayout -> "Column"], After, Identity]])(*,*)(*"1:eJylUk9PE0EUL4IFiSbKuZD14HGjttXCgWwKVFOzRGQb7rM7b+qk0xk6OwuUcOVD6JUbn4Czl948cOEDwMWYmPgNfDMTIW0whPgOv+y8fe/9fu/P81Rts+lSqZQ/QdjhsL8BmdLEKJ3MoieGLkha9SHzCC3K8Z8NZFPWt4DwTitpWpK2DiArDEkFJC+sm0D1DSGkGlbrjVdhffl1PVymhIUrwN7SRiNbqdUIe2CrzCBsF5g3Zz+A0I9SDJ23owuYiLEyEhCQOar8oaMSOXiRZYQtQTKgrPxXdMwl+E5uSsU8Nz7jEcIG11iP74Hvyrq2FJcm4YegF0eDymhwFPlwJ/H92roSSuuzpeOfn86+R7rm7DLSX79Y+xH5Qs8QmmmuRGGg85lnPQl5zq2I/+dmzn5F+vT3+Wb69CrSq/MXJ7ur3+7mHptCYhnDWHU7wcuAJhV8tQ3gDaCkANP3QAdM6UAGRNKgN74Ndzd+tptE90DnEyMee90sy7XZLIzqI0923yjHbNf7AQcFE1u9vpt/HJA/CZKCSMxQACvdrteFPr7uLiZDVZjEkuL4i750KpsMJ+XW0qYgDTfDP0012v0="*)(*]VB*)

For this relatively thick sample, we cannot observe a significant difference. However, the difference may become critical for submillimeter samples. Let's compare the real parts of the refractive indices as well.

Fabry–Pérot deconvolution

Finally, to take full advantage of the time-domain method, we should deconvolve the material parameters from the internal reflections that produce oscillatory patterns in all spectra. To enable deconvolution, simply set:

Method->{"Iterative", "SolveFP"->True}

However, this usually does not work on the first attempt. FP deconvolution is extremely sensitive to slight inaccuracies in thickness measurements or differences in aperture between the sample and reference. Therefore, we need to vary "Gain" and thickness slightly, as well as the static phase shift "PhaseCorrection". Note that "PhaseCorrection" can only be ±Z 2π\pm Z ~ 2\pi±Z 2π; it originates from noisy low-frequency data, which can produce such phase jumps. This is essentially a multivariable optimization problem.

To find the best (or true) combination, we use an estimated value generated by EstimateMaterialParameter["FP Reduction"], which is essentially the relative amplitude of the FP oscillations compared with the background. Here, we find it using a grid search:

Module[{band = Interval[{(*VB[*)(Quantity[1.5, "Terahertz"])(*,*)(*"1:eJxTTMoPSmNkYGAoZgESHvk5KWnMIB4vkAjLTC13SU3OL0osyS8K5gCKBJYm5pVkllQWMYDBD/tgTiAVklqUmJFaVFIFAKruE0k="*)(*]VB*), (*VB[*)(Quantity[2.5, "Terahertz"])(*,*)(*"1:eJxTTMoPSmNkYGAoZgESHvk5KWnMIB4vkAjLTC13SU3OL0osyS8K5gCKBJYm5pVkllQWMYABi0MwJ5AKSS1KzEgtKqkCAJu9ElY="*)(*]VB*)}], temporal = {}}, Monitor[Table[ temporal = Append[temporal, {d, gain, EstimateMaterialParameter["FP Reduction", unwrapped, Quantity[d, "Millimeters"], "Gain" -> gain, "FPInterval" -> band]}]; temporal[[-1]], {d, 0.6, 0.7, 0.0025}, {gain, 0.5,1.6,0.05}], ListDensityPlot[temporal, PlotRange->{{0.6,0.7}, {0.5,1.6}}] ] ]; ListContourPlot[data = Flatten[%, 1], FrameLabel->{"Thickness (mm)", "Gain"}, PlotRange->Full] MaximalBy[data, Last] (*VB[*)(FrontEndRef["F20cc474e-058d-4d48-a981-1a92b6bd38b1"])(*,*)(*"1:eJxTTMoPSmNkYGAoZgESHvk5KRCeEJBwK8rPK3HNS3GtSE0uLUlMykkNVgUJGxkkJ5uYm6TqGphapOiapJhY6CZaWhjqGiZaGiWZJaUYWyQZAgCVIBW3"*)(*]VB*) {{0.6375`,1.2`,11.101126070616184`}}

The global minimum is {0.637, 1.2}. Let's subtract the FP contribution and compare it with the previous results:

Circular basis (MCD, NCD, and others)

Our library can transform data acquired with linearly polarized light, using a special arrangement of polarizer and analyzer angles, to retrieve the circular components of the light. This is helpful when the eigenstates of light inside the probed medium are circularly polarized (as in Faraday rotation, MCD, and other effects). In this example, the data were measured at a fixed polarizer angle in two subsequent measurements with Analyzer=Polarizer±45∘\text{Analyzer} = \text{Polarizer}\pm 45^\circAnalyzer=Polarizer±45∘.

All transformations are performed in the time domain. Here is an example:

(* LOAD YOUR DATA *) (* here we use example data stored in the notebook *) {sam, ref} = NotebookRead[NotebookStore["contradictoriness-06c"]]; sam = QuantityArray[#, {"Picoseconds", 1}] &/@ sam; ref = QuantityArray[#, {"Picoseconds", 1}] &/@ ref;

This effectively switches the basis from linear to circular:

sam = LinearProjectionsToCircular[Sequence@@sam, {-45Degree, 45Degree}]; ref = LinearProjectionsToCircular[Sequence@@ref, {-45Degree, 45Degree}];

sam and ref can now be treated as usual, including for material-parameter extraction and Fabry–Pérot deconvolution, provided that the original data were measured using circularly polarized light.

t = MapThread[DeconvolveTraces[#1, #2]&, {sam, ref}]; EstimateMaterialParameter["\[Alpha]", FrequencySpectrumTrim[#], Quantity[0.08, "Millimeters"]] &/@ t; ListLinePlot[%, PlotRange->{{0.5,3.0}, {-150, 300}}, Frame->True, PlotStyle->{Red,Blue}, PlotLegends->{ "CW", "CCW" }] (*VB[*)(Legended[ToExpression[FrontEndRef["F7e5a2714-a0d1-42a9-b233-352ec93a458f"], InputForm], Placed[LineLegend[{Directive[PointSize[0.006944444444444445], AbsoluteThickness[2], RGBColor[1, 0, 0]], Directive[PointSize[0.006944444444444445], AbsoluteThickness[2], RGBColor[0, 0, 1]]}, {"CW", "CCW"}, LegendMarkers -> {{False, Automatic}, {False, Automatic}}, Joined -> {True, True}, LabelStyle -> {}, LegendLayout -> "Column"], After, Identity]])(*,*)(*"1:eJy1Uk1PAjEQXb/wI3rQsx48eNxEdiHIyeCCRrNGQomcu7tTbShtaLvqGv8ff8t+BAhEDx68vLTTmXnvzfQ8EwOyFQSBOjLwTOG9C7mQWAuJdk0khRfgReRTDgz0CmrebCLZsLETA7dScN3jRe8D8lLjjAG6sOEWNHHUqjdCfFnUw0aE22EWxXEYNyPI2zFuNK8I2bRdtg0MSlO3Zw+AiyfOKhcdyhLWcqwMBAxyR6V2LBVmCrzImoE+wzkUpDYXnVIO3smyVUqV9hX7BrpUmn70DbwrG+oLyjWinyDPZtPT2fTr2r8dG+hkSrBSw/CV5mMOSlHb17dzFu5uEsGEpLaCBnP4f74FlWNedYvsLRkhW5Uko9Wpuv37GT1iOQap1ka1clsO3UnvlFpMsKb5X7Mcs13TgzEPa9tZ7P+Xj+BXizNgSFcMSPCzXpd6uHCX4kqUGllSM7Jywp3KDtHGsh3lfQFcU119A9XEuBU="*)(*]VB*)

The signal is strongly affected by FP fringes. However, we can attempt to remove them and compare the results.

Quantity[0.08, "Millimeters"], Method->{"Iterative", "SolveFP"->fp}, "PhaseCorrection"->#2, "Gain"->0.6 ] ], Function[xy, xy[[1]]>=0.5 && xy[[1]]<=3.2]] &, {unwrapped, {-4Pi,0}}], FrameLabel->{"\[Omega] (THz)", "\[Alpha] (1/cm)"}, PlotRange->{{0.5,3.0}, Automatic}, Frame->True, PlotStyle->{Red,Blue}, PlotLegends->{"CW", "CCW"}] ]}, Row[{ Labeled[estimate[True], "After", Top],
